newsitem.title: USA: June 2 set for U.S. flight attendants tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: June 2 set for U.S. flight attendants tobacco suit.

text.p: A huge second-hand smoke suit brought by flight attendants against the tobacco industry is scheduled to go to trial on June 2, 1997 in the first class action case against cigarette makers.
Dade County Court Judge Robert Kaye, who rejected the tobacco industry's efforts to delay the proceeding until 1998, set a firm trial date on Friday.

"We are on track. June 2 is not a target date, it's a trial date. The judge has set aside eight weeks," Stanley Rosenblatt, attorney for the flight attendants, told Reuters. "We're very happy. This will give us time to give notice."

The 1991 lawsuit, Broin v. Philip Morris Cos. Inc., was filed on behalf of all flight attendants claiming injury from inhaling passengers' smoke. The number of attendants affected by smoke could be as high as 60,000, Rosenblatt has estimated.

"That's fabulous. I'm obviously very delighted," Norma Broin, an American Airlines attendant, said of the trial date. "This has been five years getting to this point and it looked like it could have got dragged out forever," she said by telephone from her home in Stafford, Virginia.
Barry Davidson, a lawyer representing Philip Morris, said he was concerned the judge did not realise how much work needed to be done to prepare for the trial.
"The manner in which it has to be tried has also yet to be decided. Notice has not yet gone out to people whose rights are to be decided," he said, adding: "We'll do whatever's necessary."
Kaye has signed an order requiring airlines to furnish information so that possible participants in the suit can be tracked down to determine if they wish to participate.
Rosenblatt said he expected at least 200,000 serving and former flight attendants to be notified. Northwest Airlines has already supplied a list containing 103,000 names.
The Florida Supreme Court last week allowed a class action brought by smokers in the state to move forward. That case, Engle v. R.J. Reynolds, also was filed by Rosenblatt.
In its ruling, the court refused to hear an appeal by the tobacco industry of the certification of class action status in that case.

The largest class action ever filed against the tobacco industry, Castano v. The American Tobacco Co., was thrown out by a New Orleans federal appeals court in May. The court found that the case, brought on behalf of all smokers alleging injury from cigarettes, would have been too cumbersome if brought to trial.
